title: 01 — Why Polars Is Fast
html:
01 — Why Polars Is Fast

The one idea: Polars is fast when the work stays inside the engine: columns of typed values processed by compiled code on every core. The moment you hand it a Python function per row, you are back to Python speed, or slower.

1. What it is

Layer Plain Python pandas Polars
Data layout A list of objects, each value a boxed Python object NumPy arrays per column (object arrays for strings) Apache Arrow columns: contiguous, typed, null bitmaps
Execution The interpreter, one bytecode at a time Vectorised C for many operations, mostly one core Rust kernels, vectorised and multithreaded by default
Planning None None: each line runs immediately Optional query optimiser (lazy API, 02)
Strings Python str objects Python objects in an array (or Arrow strings when enabled) Arrow string views, no Python objects 
---
title: Where the time goes in each approach
---
flowchart LR
    A["Plain Python loop"] --> A1["Interpreter per row<br/>(boxing, dict lookups)"]
    B["pandas"] --> B1["C loops per column<br/>(single core)"]
    C["Polars expressions"] --> C1["Optimised plan"] --> C2["Rust kernels<br/>on all cores"]
    D["Polars map_elements"] --> D1["Python call per row<br/>(holds the GIL)"]

2. Why it matters

  • The same pipeline can run several times faster and use a fraction of the memory, so it fits on a laptop instead of a cluster.
  • Expressions are also easier to test and to read than loops with mutable state.
  • But the speed is not automatic. Code written in a row-by-row style throws it away.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Think in columns, not rows

An expression (pl.col("qty") * pl.col("price")) describes a column computation. Polars runs it over the whole column in compiled code. Several expressions in one select or with_columns run in parallel.

3.2 Contexts

Context Use
select Pick or compute columns. The result has only these columns
with_columns Add or replace columns, keep the rest
filter Keep rows where an expression is true
group_by(...).agg(...) One row per group. Every expression in agg runs per group, in parallel

3.3 Conditional logic without if

pl.when(cond).then(a).otherwise(b) replaces an if inside a loop. Chain .when for more branches.

3.4 The escape hatches, and their cost

Tool Speed Use when
Built-in expressions (str, dt, list, struct namespaces) Fastest Almost always. Check the API first
map_batches (a function on the whole column, e.g. a NumPy ufunc) Fast if the function is vectorised A library function works on arrays
map_elements (a Python function per value) Slow: Python speed, one core, plus conversion overhead Nothing else exists, the data is small
Expression plugins (Rust) Native speed You need custom logic at scale

4. Working code

Two million trades, the net signed amount per account, done four ways. Every approach must give the same answer.

import time
import pandas as pd
import polars as pl

# 2 million trades: account, side, quantity, price. Same data for every approach.
n = 2_000_000
df = pl.DataFrame({
    "account": pl.int_range(n, eager=True) % 1_000,
    "side": pl.Series(["BUY", "SELL"] * (n // 2)),
    "qty": (pl.int_range(n, eager=True) * 7919 % 500) + 1,
    "price": ((pl.int_range(n, eager=True) * 104_729 % 10_000) / 100).cast(pl.Float64),
})
rows = df.rows()                 # plain Python tuples for the loop version
pdf = df.to_pandas()

def timed(label, fn):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = fn()
    print(f"{label:<34} {time.perf_counter() - start:7.3f} s")
    return result

def python_loop():
    totals = {}
    for account, side, qty, price in rows:
        signed = qty * price if side == "BUY" else -qty * price
        totals[account] = totals.get(account, 0.0) + signed
    return totals

def pandas_way():
    signed = pdf["qty"] * pdf["price"]
    signed = signed.where(pdf["side"] == "BUY", -signed)
    return signed.groupby(pdf["account"]).sum()

def polars_expr():
    return (
        df.group_by("account")
        .agg(
            pl.when(pl.col("side") == "BUY")
            .then(pl.col("qty") * pl.col("price"))
            .otherwise(-pl.col("qty") * pl.col("price"))
            .sum()
            .alias("net")
        )
    )

def polars_map_elements():
    # Anti-pattern: a Python function per row throws away vectorisation and threads.
    return df.with_columns(
        pl.struct("side", "qty", "price")
        .map_elements(lambda r: r["qty"] * r["price"] * (1 if r["side"] == "BUY" else -1),
                      return_dtype=pl.Float64)
        .alias("signed")
    ).group_by("account").agg(pl.col("signed").sum().alias("net"))

loop = timed("pure Python loop", python_loop)
pd_res = timed("pandas (vectorised)", pandas_way)
pl_res = timed("Polars expressions", polars_expr)
me_res = timed("Polars map_elements (anti-pattern)", polars_map_elements)

# Same answer from all four.
check = pl_res.sort("account")
assert abs(check["net"][0] - loop[0]) < 1e-6
assert abs(check["net"][0] - pd_res.loc[0]) < 1e-6
assert abs(me_res.sort("account")["net"][0] - loop[0]) < 1e-6
print("all four agree; account 0 net =", round(check["net"][0], 2))

Output:

pure Python loop                     0.221 s
pandas (vectorised)                  0.090 s
Polars expressions                   0.040 s
Polars map_elements (anti-pattern)   1.072 s
all four agree; account 0 net = 90000.0

What to notice:

  • Polars expressions are the fastest: about 5× the plain Python loop and 2× pandas here. The job is small and simple (one multiply, one sum). The gap grows with heavier work: string processing, joins, sorts, many columns, data that doesn't fit in Python objects.
  • map_elements is about 5× slower than the plain loop. It pays for the Python call per row and for converting each row into a Python dict for the struct. It is the most common way to make Polars slow.
  • All four agree, so you can migrate step by step and assert the results match.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Iterating rows (for row in df.iter_rows()) to compute something an expression could do.
  2. map_elements for logic that when/then, str.* or dt.* already covers.
  3. Calling .to_pandas() in the middle of a pipeline to use a familiar method, then converting back.
  4. One with_columns per column. Put independent expressions in one call so they run in parallel.
  5. Judging speed on tiny data. Under about 100,000 rows, overheads dominate and everything feels instant.

6. Exercise (45 minutes)

  1. Add a per-account count and average to the Polars version in one agg, and time it again.
  2. Rewrite the map_elements version with map_batches and NumPy, and compare.
  3. Increase n to 20 million and see how each approach scales (watch memory for the Python loop).

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why is a plain Python loop slow for columnar data?
  2. What does pl.when().then().otherwise() replace?
  3. Why is map_elements slower than a plain Python loop in this test?
  4. When would you write an expression plugin?
  5. Why put several expressions in one with_columns?

Answers

  1. Every value is a boxed object, and every step goes through the interpreter, on one core.
  2. An if/else inside a row loop.
  3. It adds per-row conversion into Python objects (here a dict per struct row) on top of the Python call itself.
  4. When you need custom logic at scale that no built-in expression covers.
  5. Polars evaluates them in parallel, and the plan stays in one pass.

8. Sources
